catalog_quote: Short vowels carry one mora, while long vowels carry two moras; short consonants carry no moras, while geminate consonants carry one mora. ... Stress assignment is also weight-sensitive, with primary stress assigned to the penultimate mora of a prosodic word. Secondary stress is assigned to every other mora preceding the primary stress. If one mora of a long vowel is assigned stress, stress is distributed across the entire long vowel. Geminate consonants are never assigned stress, simply by virtue of how they are formed (§3.1.3.4). Examples of stress assignment are provided in (4), where primary stress is represented by an acute accent (ˊ) and secondary stress is represented by a grave accent (ˋ). (4) Stress assignment patterns: ea 'rise' [é.a]; boo 'night' [póː]; huli 'turn' [hú.ɾi]; gidee 'see' [ki.téː]; daane 'man' [tǽː.ne]; dagodo 'lay' [ta.kó.to]; duudagi 'continue' [tùː.tá.ki]; hagaduu 'build' [hà.ka.túː]; gooluu 'you (dual)' [kòː.ɾúː]; langadala 'sleeping mat' [ɾà.ŋa.tá.ɾa] [Drummond 2023:31-32]. -- Carroll 1965:199: Primary stress (′) occurs at least once in each contour word, predictably on the penultimate syllable of each base, pronoun or other morpheme occupying the nuclear position. Reduplicated bases behave as two separate bases in this respect. Primary stress is phonetically defined by rising pitch.

Opened (485 pp., text layer; title page 'Clause structure and ergativity in Nukuoro', Emily Nicole Drummond, UC Berkeley, Fall 2023, eScholarship 1xv905sb) and re-extracted PDF pp. 46-50 (printed pp. 30-34) with extracted text myself. Sec. 3.1.1 'Phonemes, phonotactics, and stress', printed p. 31 bottom to p. 32 top, reads exactly: 'Stress assignment is also weight-sensitive, with primary stress assigned to the penultimate mora of a prosodic word. Secondary stress is assigned to every other mora preceding the primary stress. If one mora of a long vowel is assigned stress, stress is distributed across the entire long vowel. Geminate consonants are never assig…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Count moras from the right edge of the prosodic word (short V = 1 mora, long V = 2, geminate C = 1 but never stress-bearing): primary stress falls on the penultimate mora, i.e. on the penultimate syllable when the final vowel is short (dagodo [ta.kó.to], daane [tǽː.ne]) but on the final syllable when it contains a long vowel (hagaduu [hà.ka.túː], gidee [ki.téː]); a stressed mora of a long vowel makes the whole long vowel stressed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on every other mora leftward from the primary stress (duudagi [tùː.tá.ki], langadala [ɾà.ŋa.tá.ɾa], gooluu [kòː.ɾúː]).
new_statements.exceptions: None lexical. Geminate consonants (moraic) are never stressed; unstressed vowels between identical consonants syncopate to form geminates; unstressed word-final vowels devoice. In ch. 4 (ex. 20) the author marks stress without distinguishing primary/secondary.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the prosodic word, which can include determiners/particles prosodified with a content word (gemination applies across such boundaries, sec. 3.1.3.4 and ch. 4). Ch. 4 fn. 4: core arguments bear an LH* pitch contour on 'the primary stressed, penultimate mora'. Author notes the phonology section is informed by Carroll (1965a) but the dissertation rests on her own fieldwork (2015-2023).
new_statements.identity_note: Drummond 2023 describes Nukuoro as spoken on Nukuoro Atoll and by the diaspora on Pohnpei (fieldwork 2015-2023 with speakers from both); single language, no dialect split reported; matches nuku1260 / ISO nkr directly.

readall_conflicts: The one work in the list (Drummond & Rudolph 2021) is silent, so it creates no conflict. Between the sources already held by the project there is a real but minor disagreement not settled by a third reader by this work: Carroll 1965 Part I, sec. 1.4, p. 199 puts primary stress 'predictably on the penultimate syllable of each base, pronoun or other morpheme occupying the nuclear position' (a morpheme-level, syllable-counting rule, phonetically rising pitch), while Drummond 2023, sec. 3.1.1, pp. 31-32 (existing_statement) puts primary stress on the penultimate mora of the prosodic word with secondary stress on every other preceding mora. The two rules differ for words containing long vowels (e.g. a final long vowel takes the stress under the mora rule but not under the syllable rule) and in domain (morpheme vs. prosodic word); Drummond 2023 is the more recent and more explicit analysis and is the basis for the weight-sensitive reading.

sources.note: Sec. 3.1.1 'Phonemes, phonotactics, and stress' (pp. 31-32): stress is weight-sensitive; primary stress on the penultimate mora of the prosodic word; secondary stress on every other mora preceding; stress on one mora of a long vowel spreads over the whole long vowel; geminates never stressed; ten worked examples (e.g. hagaduu [hà.ka.túː], daane [tǽː.ne], langadala [ɾà.ŋa.tá.ɾa]). Ch. 4 fn. 4 adds that core arguments carry an LH* contour on 'the primary stressed, penultimate mora'; unstressed word-final vowels devoice.
